entries.meaning: Vasiṣṭha replied: ‘Dear child, your words are true through Rāma’s grace; no accomplishment comes even in a dream to one opposed to him. I hesitate to say one thing, though the wise sometimes surrender half to save the whole: you and Śatrughna should go to the forest, and Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and Raghurāya should be sent back.’ Hearing this excellent proposal, the two brothers rejoiced and their bodies filled with delight. Hearts bright and bodies radiant, they seemed inwardly to behold King Rāma already enthroned. The people would gain much for little loss; equal in pain and pleasure, only the queens wept for them all. The company said the sage’s plan should be done, for it gave every creature the desired fruit. Bharata declared he would live his whole life in the forest; no greater good fortune could be his. ‘Rāma and Sītā know every heart and you are omniscient; if you truly speak this, Lord, please make your word authoritative.’

Hearing Bharata and seeing his love, the sage and whole assembly lost bodily awareness. Bharata’s immense glory was an ocean and the sage’s understanding a helpless woman standing on its shore, wishing to cross but finding neither boat, ship, nor raft. Who else could praise Bharata—can a small lake or shell contain the sea? Bharata pleased the sage inwardly, and they came with the assembly before Rāma. The Lord bowed and offered him a fine seat; everyone sat at the sage’s direction. Bharadvāja then spoke after weighing country, time, and occasion: ‘Hear me, omniscient Rāma, treasury of duty, policy, virtue, and knowledge. You dwell within every heart and know both good and bad intentions. Please state the means that will benefit the citizens, mothers, and Bharata.’

The distressed do not deliberate, Rāma said; a gambler sees only his own throw. Hearing the sage, Raghurāya added: ‘Lord, the means rests entirely in your hands. Everyone’s welfare will follow if your preference is honored, your command obeyed, and truth spoken gladly. Whatever instruction first falls to me, I shall place upon my head and carry out; then whatever you tell each person, each will fulfill in every way through service.’ The sage answered: ‘Rāma, what you say is true, yet you have not considered Bharata’s love. Again and again I speak because my understanding has come under the power of his devotion. In my judgment, whatever is done while honoring Bharata’s wish will be auspicious—Śiva bears witness. Hear Bharata’s humble petition respectfully and consider it once more; we shall distill the opinion of saints and people, royal policy, and scripture.’

Seeing the guru’s love for Bharata, special joy arose in Rāma’s heart. Knowing Bharata to bear duty’s weight and to be his servant in body, mind, and speech, he answered the guru in lovely, gentle, auspicious words: ‘Lord, by my father’s feet I swear that no brother like Bharata has arisen in the world. Those devoted to the guru’s lotus feet are greatly fortunate in world and Veda alike. Who can express Bharata’s fortune when you hold such love for him?’ Seeing his younger brother’s modest, discerning silence, Rāma openly praised him, then concluded: ‘Whatever Bharata says should be done; therein lies welfare.’ The sage then told Bharata: ‘Dear child, abandon every hesitation and speak the heart’s desire to your beloved, compassionate brother.’

Hearing the sage, perceiving Rāma’s inclination, and finding guru and master wholly favorable, Bharata saw the whole difficult burden laid upon his head. Unable to speak, he reflected. His body thrilled as he rose in the assembly; tears of affection swelled in his lotus eyes. ‘The sage-lord has fulfilled all I could say—what more can I add? I know my own master’s nature: he is never angry even with an offender and has shown me particular grace and love. Even in childhood games I never saw him annoyed with me. From infancy he never left my company or broke my heart; observing my Lord’s gracious way, I saw him let me win even when I had lost a game. Bound by love and reserve, I did not speak openly even then; and to this day sight has not satisfied these eyes thirsty for love.’

Bharata continued: ‘Destiny could not endure my Lord’s fondness and, using my low mother as a pretext, placed an obstruction between us. Even saying this does not suit me today: considering my own nature, who could call me holy and pure? To imagine that my mother is wicked while I am saintly and well-conducted would itself be one of millions of crooked thoughts. Can millet bear fine rice, or a black shell produce a pearl? Not even the slightest fault belongs to anyone; the unfathomable ocean is my misfortune. Without understanding the ripened fruit of my own sin, I burned in going about crying against my mother. I searched my heart in every direction and found only one way my good may truly become good: guru, protector, master, Sītā, and Rāma are favorable, and the outcome appears good to me. Before this holy assembly, guru, and Lord I speak pure truth from a fitting place; sage and Raghurāya know whether it is love, deceit, falsehood, or truth.’

‘The king kept his vow of love by dying, and the whole world witnessed my mother’s evil counsel. The mothers cannot be looked upon in their distress; men and women of the city burn in unbearable fever. Hearing and understanding that I am the root of every calamity upon earth, I endured all these spears. Then I heard Raghunātha had gone to the forest with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā in ascetic dress, barefoot and on foot. Śiva is witness that I still survived this wound. When I next beheld the Niṣāda’s affection, my thunderbolt-hard heart did not split. Now I have come and seen everything with my own eyes; every inert support keeps my life alive. Even snakes and scorpions on the road would abandon their fierce, piercing poison upon seeing those Raghunandanas, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā. Why does destiny force unbearable pain upon the son of one who acted against them?’

Hearing Bharata’s excellent, anguished words steeped in love, humility, and wisdom, the whole assembly became silent and sorrowful, like a lotus grove struck by frost. The wise sage consoled him with many ancient accounts. Then Rāma, the moon to the night-blooming lilies of the Solar line, spoke fitting words: ‘Dear Bharata, do not burden your heart with shame; know the living being’s course rests with the Lord. In all three times and the three worlds, according to me, no one’s holy fame stands above yours. Merely entertaining crookedness toward you destroys both this world and the next. Only dull people who have never served guru, saint, or assembly blame your mother. All burdens of sin, deceit, and misfortune will disappear; remembering your name brings fair fame here and happiness hereafter.’

Rāma continued: ‘I tell my true nature with Śiva as witness: the earth and its kingdom are being preserved for you. Dear brother, do not form useless suspicions; enmity and love cannot remain hidden however one hides them. Birds and animals approach groups of sages, but flee on seeing a trapper or hunter. Even beasts and birds know friend and foe; the human body is a treasury of virtue and knowledge. I know you thoroughly, so why should I create this needless uncertainty? Our father protected truth by abandoning me and cast off his body while holding fast to love’s vow. My heart grieves to break his word, yet your restraint grieves me even more. Beyond this, the guru has commanded me; whatever you say, I certainly wish to do. Make your mind glad, abandon hesitation, and tell me—I shall do it today.’ The whole assembly rejoiced to hear Raghubara’s truth-bound words.

The gods and frightened Indra worried that the desired obstruction was about to fail. Finding no effective device, they all inwardly sought Rāma’s refuge. Reflecting together, they said: ‘Raghupati and his devotees are bound by devotion. Remember Ambarīṣa and Durvāsas’: the gods and Indra became utterly hopeless. The gods had long endured grief until Narasiṃha appeared for Prahlāda. Leaning ear to ear and beating their foreheads, they whispered: ‘Now the gods’ purpose rests in Bharata’s hands. No other means is visible, for Rāma submits to the service of a perfect servant. Let us all lovingly remember Bharata, whose own virtue and character bring Rāma under his sway.’ Hearing the divine opinion, Bṛhaspati said: ‘Good! Great is your fortune—love for Bharata’s feet is the root of every blessing in the world.’
